setup.zh: 出村时，吴婆婆把一块磨亮的木牌塞给你：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」前山满地狗爪印——马家的围猎篦空了它。
setup.en: Leaving the village, Granny Wu pressed a worn token into your hand: "When you reach the stele, look at its back." The front slopes are all dog tracks — the Mas' hunts combed them bare.

recap.zh: 吴婆婆给了你一块狐纹木牌；前山被马家的围猎篦空了，只打着一只山鸡；晌午，你在松树上望见黑松岭林子边一头鹿。
recap.en: Granny Wu gave you a fox-carved token; the Mas' hunts had combed the front slopes bare — one pheasant all morning; at noon, from a pine, you saw a deer at the edge of Black Pine Ridge.

zh: 村东头，瞎眼的吴婆婆，像在等你们。
一块磨得发亮的小木牌。
前山：满地狗爪印，马蹄印。
en: At the east end, blind Granny Wu, as if she were waiting.
A little wooden token, worn bright.
The front slopes: dog tracks and hoofprints everywhere.

text.zh: 木牌磨得发亮，刻着一只蜷着的狐狸，尾巴一圈圈绕着身子；入手比看着沉，凉丝丝的。
text.en: The tablet is rubbed smooth: a curled fox, its tail wound round and round its body. It is heavier in the hand than it looks, and cool.

text.zh: 狗爪印、马蹄印一层叠着一层，连兔子洞都给刨开了——马家篦过的山，连根兔毛都不剩。
text.en: Dog prints and hoofprints lie layer on layer; even the rabbit holes are dug open. Where the Mas have combed a hill, not a rabbit hair is left.

story.zh:
井台边蹲着一个半大孩子，是老刘家的大小子刘豆芽，瞧见爷儿俩背着弓往山里去，眼珠子转了一转。[吴婆婆]{注=wupo}照旧坐在门槛上，一双白蒙蒙的眼睛朝着山的方向，仿佛专门在等他们。吴婆婆是石坳村最老的人，眼睛看不见，耳朵却比村里所有的狗加起来还灵。她问道：「去黑松岭？」小满他爹没吭声。

吴婆婆摸索着从怀里掏出一样东西，塞进小满手里，却是一块小木牌，磨得发亮，上面刻着一只蜷着的狐狸。她道：「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过。」

吴婆婆又道：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」小满问：「看什么？」吴婆婆笑了，露出仅剩的三颗牙，道：「看了，就知道了。不看，就不知道。」小满还是把木牌揣进了怀里。他娘说过，老人家说话，十句里有九句是废话，剩下那一句，能救命。

弓是小满爷爷传下来的，弓背裂过两回，拿牛筋缠着。小满小时候问过一回，爷爷没回来，弓怎么回来的。他爹只说了一句：「你爷爷没回来。弓回来了。」至于腿，他爹的膝盖不行了，这两年，腿是小满的。

那一天，父子两个天没亮就进了山。前山什么也没有，满地都是狗爪印、马蹄印。原来马家入秋办了三场围猎，带着二十条猎狗、几十个家丁，把前山篦了一遍又一遍，篦得比他娘梳头还细。
story.en:
By the well platform squatted a half-grown boy, Beansprout Liu, the eldest of old Liu's family. He saw father and son heading for the mountains with a bow on their backs, and his eyes flicked this way and that. [Granny Wu]{注=wupo} sat on her doorstep as usual, her clouded white eyes turned towards the mountain, as if she'd been waiting for them specially. Granny Wu was the oldest person in Shi'ao Village. Her eyes couldn't see, but her ears were sharper than all the village dogs put together. She asked, "Going to Black Pine Ridge?" Xiaoman's father didn't make a sound.

Granny Wu fumbled something out of the front of her jacket and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand. It was a little wooden tablet, rubbed shiny, carved with a curled-up fox. She said, "The year your grandpa went, he passed my door too."

Granny Wu said, "When you get to the stone, look at the back of it." Xiaoman asked, "Look at what?" Granny Wu smiled, showing her last three teeth. "Look, and you'll know. Don't look, and you won't." He tucked the tablet inside his jacket anyway. His mother said that of every ten things old people say, nine are nonsense, and the one left over can save your life.

The bow had come down from Xiaoman's grandpa. Its back had cracked twice and was wrapped in ox sinew. Once, when he was small, Xiaoman had asked: if Grandpa never came back, how did the bow come back? His father said only, "Your grandpa didn't come back. The bow did." As for the legs — his father's knee was no good now, and these last two years the legs had been Xiaoman's.

That day father and son went into the mountains before it was light. The near hills had nothing in them. The ground was all dog prints and hoof prints. The Mas had held three hunts since autumn began, with twenty hounds and dozens of men, and combed the near hills over and over, finer than his mother combed her hair.

story_full.zh:
出村要经过村东头。井台边蹲着一个半大孩子，是老刘家的大小子刘豆芽，细脖子顶着个大脑袋，真像一根豆芽，正在收麻雀网，瞧见爷儿俩背着弓往山里去，眼珠子转了一转。[吴婆婆]{注=wupo}照旧坐在门槛上，一双白蒙蒙的眼睛朝着山的方向，仿佛专门在等他们。吴婆婆是石坳村最老的人，眼睛看不见，耳朵却比村里所有的狗加起来还灵。

谁家半夜偷了谁家的瓜，她第二天一早便知道，不但知道是谁偷的，还知道偷了几个，连哪个是生的都知道。小满小时候，马家在村口摆寿宴，锣鼓敲了一整天，她在门槛上听了一整天，末了只说了一句：「马家那一家子，吃了还饿。」

她问道：「去黑松岭？」小满他爹没吭声。

吴婆婆也不要他们回答，自顾自地道：「蒙山顶上从前住过一个骑白鹤的老头，一顿饭吃一颗枣，活了八百岁。」他爹道：「婆婆，我们赶路。」吴婆婆道：「嗯。他也赶路。」他爹便不再搭话，低头对小满道：「编的。」

吴婆婆摸索着从怀里掏出一样东西，塞进小满手里，却是一块小木牌，磨得发亮，上面刻着一只蜷着的狐狸。那木头黑里透着一点银，不知是什么木，入手比看着沉，凉丝丝的；凑到鼻子底下，有一股极淡的香，像下过雨的松林，又像别的什么，小满说不上来。她道：「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过。」

小满张了张嘴，一个字也没说出来。

吴婆婆又道：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」小满问：「看什么？」吴婆婆笑了，露出仅剩的三颗牙，道：「看了，就知道了。不看，就不知道。」

小满觉得这句话说了跟没说一样，可还是把木牌揣进了怀里。他娘说过，老人家说话，十句里有九句是废话，剩下那一句，能救命。

小满他爹常说，打猎的人家有三样东西不能少：一张好弓，一双好腿，一副好耳朵。弓是小满爷爷传下来的，弓背裂过两回，拿牛筋缠着，远远看过去，像一条打了补丁的裤子。小满小时候问过一回，爷爷没回来，弓怎么回来的。

他爹只说了一句：「你爷爷没回来。弓回来了。」再问，便是「吃饭」。耳朵是他爹的，他能听见三里外一只獐子踩断一根枯枝。

至于腿，他爹的膝盖不行了，这两年，腿是小满的。

那一天，父子两个天没亮就进了山。前山什么也没有，满地都是狗爪印、马蹄印。原来马家入秋办了三场围猎，带着二十条猎狗、几十个家丁，把前山篦了一遍又一遍，篦得比他娘梳头还细。
story_full.en:
The way out of the village went past its east end. By the well platform squatted a half-grown boy, Beansprout Liu, the eldest of old Liu's family — a thin neck holding up a big head, exactly like a beansprout — taking in his sparrow net. He saw father and son heading for the mountains with a bow on their backs, and his eyes flicked this way and that. [Granny Wu]{注=wupo} sat on her doorstep as usual, her clouded white eyes turned towards the mountain, as if she'd been waiting for them specially. Granny Wu was the oldest person in Shi'ao Village. Her eyes couldn't see, but her ears were sharper than all the village dogs put together.

If someone stole someone's melons in the night, she knew first thing next morning — knew not just who'd done it but how many, and even which ones weren't ripe. When Xiaoman was little, the Mas had held a birthday banquet at the village gate, with gongs and drums going all day; she'd listened from her doorstep all day, and at the end of it said just one thing: "That Ma lot. They eat and they're still hungry."

She asked, "Going to Black Pine Ridge?" Xiaoman's father didn't make a sound.

Granny Wu didn't want an answer anyway. She went on to herself: "Once upon a time there lived an old man on top of Mount Meng who rode a white crane. He ate one jujube a meal and lived to eight hundred." His father said, "Granny, we've got a way to go." Granny Wu said, "Mm. So did he." His father didn't answer that. He bent his head to Xiaoman and said, "Made up."

Granny Wu fumbled something out of the front of her jacket and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand. It was a little wooden tablet, rubbed shiny, carved with a curled-up fox. The wood was black with a touch of silver in it — what wood, he didn't know — heavier in the hand than it looked, and cool. Held under his nose it had a very faint scent, like a pine wood after rain, and like something else, though Xiaoman couldn't say what. She said, "The year your grandpa went, he passed my door too."

Xiaoman opened his mouth and not a word came out.

Granny Wu said, "When you get to the stone, look at the back of it." Xiaoman asked, "Look at what?" Granny Wu smiled, showing her last three teeth. "Look, and you'll know. Don't look, and you won't."

Xiaoman felt that this was the same as saying nothing at all, but he tucked the tablet inside his jacket anyway. His mother said that of every ten things old people say, nine are nonsense, and the one left over can save your life.

Xiaoman's father often said there were three things a hunting family couldn't do without: a good bow, a good pair of legs, and a good pair of ears. The bow had come down from Xiaoman's grandpa. Its back had cracked twice and was wrapped in ox sinew, and from a distance it looked like a pair of patched trousers. Once, when he was small, Xiaoman had asked: if Grandpa never came back, how did the bow come back?

His father said only, "Your grandpa didn't come back. The bow did." Ask again, and it was "Eat your food." The ears were his father's; he could hear a river deer snap a dry twig three li off.

As for the legs — his father's knee was no good now, and these last two years the legs had been Xiaoman's.

That day father and son went into the mountains before it was light. The near hills had nothing in them. The ground was all dog prints and hoof prints. The Mas had held three hunts since autumn began, with twenty hounds and dozens of men, and combed the near hills over and over, finer than his mother combed her hair.

label.en: Climb the tallest pine and look out

exits.means: climbs a tree to look out over the mountain, scouts, looks around

story.zh:
小满爬上最高的那棵松树，四下里望了半天，溜下来只说了一句：「爹。前山空了。」他爹道：「空到什么地步？」小满道：「连耗子都搬家了。门口还贴了告示。」他爹道：「……写的什么？」小满道：「『马家在此，无鼠可活』。」

他爹忽然站住了，把背上那张弓解下来，道：「今儿教你一样东西。」他爹道：「这是你爷爷传下来的，叫《落雁三箭》。」小满道：「落雁？爹，你射下过大雁？」他爹道：「没有。」

他爹道：「是三句话。一箭一句。今年教头一箭。」说着把弓往地下一拄，一个字一个字地道：「**先看风，后看鹿。**」小满道：「就六个字？」他爹道：「你爷爷教我，也是六个字。」

只见四十来步外一片乱草坡上，一只山鸡正低着头在草根里刨食。他爹却不忙着拉弓，先看草。一阵风从坡上刮过来，草尖一齐伏倒，他不动；风过去了，草尖晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——便在草尖将直未直的那一霎，那张打了补丁的弓在他手里一气张满，只听得「嗖」的一声，那山鸡已翻倒在草里。

小满道：「爹，你箭都搭上了，还等什么？」他爹道：「等风歇一口气。」小满道：「风还会歇气？」他爹道：「什么东西都要歇气。风也是，鹿也是，人也是。」顿了一顿，又道：「马三也是。」

昨天傍晚，他爹跪在马三跟前，两只手按在地下，是抖的；今天他爹拉开这张弓，两只手稳稳当当，连弓弦都没颤一颤。原来他爹这一双手，并不是天生会抖的。

一只山鸡，抵不了一张鹿皮。小满又爬上一棵松树去望。隔着两道山梁，是一片黑压压的松林，那便是黑松岭了。先看风——树梢往他背后歪，风是从林子那边吹过来的。黑松底下，一个赭红的影子低着头，慢慢地抬了起来，头顶上支棱着一丛什么，像冬天的枯树枝。

「爹，有鹿。」他爹一下子站了起来，膝盖也顾不得了。一头鹿，是一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，是墙上那张弓。顺着蹄印钻过一片荆棵子，眼前便是一块断碑。
story.en:
Xiaoman climbed the tallest pine and looked all round for a long time, then slid down and said only: "Pa. The near hills are empty." His father said, "How empty?" Xiaoman said, "Even the rats have moved out. They left a notice on the door." His father said, "…Saying what?" Xiaoman said, "'The Mas Are Here. No Rat Can Live.'"

His father suddenly stopped, took the bow off his back, and said, "Today I'll teach you something." His father said, "This came down from your grandpa. It's called *Three Arrows That Bring Down the Goose*." Xiaoman said, "Bring down the goose? Pa, have you ever shot down a wild goose?" His father said, "No."

His father said, "It's three sayings. One arrow, one saying. This year it's the first arrow." He planted the bow on the ground and said, one word at a time: "**First read the wind, then read the deer.**" Xiaoman said, "Just those few words?" His father said, "When your grandpa taught me, it was those few words too."

Forty-odd paces off, on a slope of tangled grass, a pheasant had its head down, scratching for food among the roots. His father didn't hurry to draw. First he read the grass. A gust swept down the slope and the grass tips all lay flat together; he didn't move. The gust passed, the grass tips wavered twice and slowly rose — and in the instant when they were nearly upright but not quite, that patched bow in his hands came to full draw in one breath. There was a *whoosh*, and the pheasant had turned over in the grass.

Xiaoman said, "Pa, you already had the arrow on the string. What were you waiting for?" His father said, "For the wind to catch its breath." Xiaoman said, "The wind catches its breath?" His father said, "Everything has to catch its breath. The wind does, deer do, people do." He paused, then said, "Ma San does too."

Yesterday evening, kneeling in front of Ma San, his father's two hands pressed on the ground had been shaking. Today, drawing this bow, his father's two hands had been steady as rock, and the bowstring hadn't so much as quivered. So his father's hands hadn't been born shaking after all.

One pheasant couldn't stand in for a deer hide. He climbed another pine to look. Two ridges away lay a pine forest, black and dense. That was Black Pine Ridge. First read the wind — the treetops leaned behind him; the wind was blowing from the forest towards him. Under the black pines a reddish-brown shape that had had its head down slowly raised it, and on top of its head stood up a cluster of something, like bare winter branches.

"Pa, there's a deer." His father was on his feet at once, knee or no knee. One deer was one deer hide and twenty catties of meat; it was the bow on the wall. They followed the prints through a thicket of thorn scrub, and in front of them stood a broken stone.

story_full.zh:
小满爬上最高的那棵松树，四下里望了半天，溜下来只说了一句：「爹。前山空了。」

他爹道：「空到什么地步？」小满道：「连耗子都搬家了。门口还贴了告示。」他爹道：「……写的什么？」小满道：「『马家在此，无鼠可活』。」

前山既然空了，他爹便领着他往山里头走。走了一程，他爹忽然站住了，把背上那张弓解下来，拿在手里掂了一掂，道：「今儿教你一样东西。」小满登时来了精神。

那张弓在他爹手里使了几十年，小满摸过它的弓背，数过弓背上缠了几道牛筋，却从来没有拉过它，他爹不许。

他爹道：「这是你爷爷传下来的，叫《落雁三箭》。」小满道：「落雁？爹，你射下过大雁？」他爹道：「没有。」小满道：「那爷爷射下过？」

他爹想了一想，道：「也没有。你爷爷那年去镇上卖皮子，听说书先生讲什么『一箭落雁』，回来便给咱家这点本事起了个名儿。他说，起了名儿，就算武功了。」顿了一顿，又道：「那说书的还讲李广射石头，射进去了。你爷爷回来也射了一块。箭断了，一支箭，削一个晚上。」从那以后，沈家只射活的。

小满道：「那它到底是不是武功？」他爹道：「是三句话。一箭一句。你爷爷教我，一年只教一箭；我教你，也一年只教一箭。今年教头一箭。」说着把弓往地下一拄，一个字一个字地道：「**先看风，后看鹿。**」

小满等了一会儿，见他没有下文，问道：「……完了？」他爹道：「完了。」小满道：「就六个字？」他爹道：「你爷爷教我，也是六个字。」小满心想，一年六个字，照这么教将下去，等他学全了，他爹的膝盖只怕已经聊不动天了。

他爹不识字，他这一辈子没有一本书，他的书都在山里。他见儿子不服气，便蹲下来——蹲得极慢，左腿直直地伸着——拔了一根草，举到眼前。那草尖儿微微地往东南歪。他爹道：「它跟你说什么？」小满盯着看了半天：「……风从西北来。」他爹道：「你站在哪头？」小满看看自己脚底下，又看看草尖，脸一红：「上风。鹿还没瞧见，先闻见我了。」他爹点了点头，把那根草塞进他手里，不说了。小满道：「那鹿呢？」他爹道：「风看明白了，鹿就跑不了。风看不明白，鹿就是别人的了。」

便在这时，他爹忽然伸手按住了他的肩膀，下巴往前一点。只见四十来步外一片乱草坡上，一只山鸡正低着头在草根里刨食，尾巴一翘一翘的，全然不知道这世上还有他们爷儿俩。他爹却不忙着拉弓，先看草。坡上的草一阵往这边倒，一阵又直起来。

他伸出一根指头，在嘴里含了一含，举在半空停了片刻，这才一声不响地往左边绕。

他那条左腿不利索，每一步都要先拿脚尖试一试地，一步，两步，足足绕了二十来步，绕到风正顺着他箭路吹的地方，背靠着一棵老栗子树站定——他那膝盖跪不得，只能站着射。然后他搭上箭，弓只开了一半，便那么端着。

小满屏住了气，等他拉弓，他却偏偏不拉。

一阵风从坡上刮过来，草尖一齐伏倒，他不动；风过去了，草尖晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——便在草尖将直未直的那一霎，那张打了补丁的弓在他手里一气张满，弯得像一轮月牙儿，满了便放，只听得「嗖」的一声，那山鸡连扑腾都没来得及扑腾一下，已翻倒在草里。

一支箭，一只山鸡。小满奔过去把山鸡提起来，那一箭正穿在它的脖子上，不偏不倚。他爹接过箭来，先不看山鸡，拿袖子把箭头擦得干干净净，对着天光瞧了瞧箭杆直不直，这才插回箭壶里。

小满道：「爹，你箭都搭上了，还等什么？」他爹道：「等风歇一口气。」小满道：「风还会歇气？」他爹道：「什么东西都要歇气。风也是，鹿也是，人也是。」顿了一顿，又道：「马三也是。」这句话小满当时没听懂，可他觉得，这是他爹这辈子说过的最有学问的一句话，便牢牢地记住了。

还有一件事，他也记住了，只是没有说出口。昨天傍晚，他爹跪在马三跟前，两只手按在地下，是抖的；今天他爹拉开这张弓，两只手稳稳当当，连弓弦都没颤一颤。原来他爹这一双手，并不是天生会抖的。

小满道：「爹，那第二箭呢？」他爹道：「明年。」说了等于没说，小满觉得这一点，他爹倒有几分像吴婆婆。

小满不死心，心想弓拉不得，风总看得。走不多远，他学着他爹的样子，从头上拔下一根头发，捏着一头举在半空，要看它往哪边飘。那头发飘是飘了，却不往东，也不往西，一阵风过，直直地飘进了他爹嘴里。他爹「呸、呸、呸」一连吐了七八口，拿指头在舌头上刮了又刮，这才回过头来，一张黑脸拉得老长，瞪着他看。

小满道：「爹，风是往你那边吹的。」他爹道：「……我知道了。」

转到晌午，前山再没见着第二样活物。那只山鸡，便是爷儿俩一上午的全部收成，瘦得皮包骨，抱在怀里像抱着一把拖把。一只山鸡，抵不了一张鹿皮。他爹坐在一块石头上揉着膝盖，许久没有说话。

小满闲不住，又爬上一棵松树去望。前山光秃秃的，什么也没有；再往里，隔着两道山梁，是一片黑压压的松林，那便是黑松岭了。他正要溜下来，林子边上有一样东西动了一动。先看风——树梢往他背后歪，风是从林子那边吹过来的。

他屏住气再看：黑松底下，一个赭红的影子低着头，慢慢地抬了起来，头顶上支棱着一丛什么，像冬天的枯树枝。只一眨眼，那影子一转，没进林子里去了。

「爹，有鹿。」

他爹一下子站了起来，膝盖也顾不得了。一头鹿，是一张鹿皮、二十斤肉，是墙上那张弓。爷儿俩认着方向一路摸过去，翻过两道山梁，摸到林子边上，泥地里果然有一溜新蹄印，又大又深，一直往林子里去。顺着蹄印钻过一片荆棵子，眼前便是一块断碑。
story_full.en:
Xiaoman climbed the tallest pine and looked all round for a long time, then slid down and said only: "Pa. The near hills are empty."

His father said, "How empty?" Xiaoman said, "Even the rats have moved out. They left a notice on the door." His father said, "…Saying what?" Xiaoman said, "'The Mas Are Here. No Rat Can Live.'"

With the near hills empty, his father led him further into the mountains. After a while his father suddenly stopped, took the bow off his back, weighed it in his hand, and said, "Today I'll teach you something." Xiaoman perked up at once. His father had used that bow for decades.

Xiaoman had touched its back and counted how many turns of ox sinew were wrapped on it, but he had never once drawn it. His father wouldn't let him.

His father said, "This came down from your grandpa. It's called *Three Arrows That Bring Down the Goose*." Xiaoman said, "Bring down the goose? Pa, have you ever shot down a wild goose?" His father said, "No." Xiaoman said, "Then did Grandpa?"

His father thought about it. "No, he didn't either. That year your grandpa went to town to sell hides and heard the storyteller going on about 'one arrow brings down the goose', and when he came back he gave our bit of skill a name. He said once it had a name it counted as martial arts." He paused, then said, "That storyteller also told how Li Guang shot a rock and the arrow went in. Your grandpa came home and shot a rock too. The arrow broke. One arrow takes a whole evening to whittle." From then on, the Shens only shot living things.

Xiaoman said, "So is it martial arts or not?" His father said, "It's three sayings. One arrow, one saying. Your grandpa taught me one arrow a year, and I'll teach you one arrow a year. This year it's the first arrow." He planted the bow on the ground and said, one word at a time: "**First read the wind, then read the deer.**"

Xiaoman waited a while, and when nothing more came, asked, "…That's it?" His father said, "That's it." Xiaoman said, "Just those few words?" His father said, "When your grandpa taught me, it was those few words too." Xiaoman thought: a few words a year — teach at that rate, and by the time he'd learned the lot, his father's knee probably wouldn't be up to chatting any more.

His father couldn't read. He hadn't owned a single book in his life; his books were all in the mountains. Seeing his son wasn't convinced, he crouched down — very slowly, his left leg stuck straight out — pulled a blade of grass and held it up in front of his eyes. The tip of the grass leaned a little to the south-east. His father said, "What's it telling you?" Xiaoman stared at it a long while. "…The wind's from the north-west." His father said, "And which end are you standing at?" Xiaoman looked down at his feet, then at the tip of the grass, and went red. "Upwind. The deer would smell me before it ever saw me." His father nodded, put the blade of grass into his hand, and said no more. Xiaoman said, "And the deer?" His father said, "Read the wind right and the deer can't get away. Read it wrong and the deer's somebody else's."

Just then his father suddenly put a hand on his shoulder and jerked his chin forward. Forty-odd paces off, on a slope of tangled grass, a pheasant had its head down, scratching for food among the roots, its tail bobbing up and down, with no idea at all that there were two such people as them in the world. His father didn't hurry to draw. First he read the grass. On the slope the grass would lean this way for a moment, then stand up straight again.

He put a finger in his mouth, held it up in the air for a moment, and then, without a sound, circled round to the left.

His left leg was awkward, and with every step he tested the ground first with his toes: one step, two steps — a good twenty-odd steps he circled, until he was where the wind blew straight along the path of his arrow, and there he set his back against an old chestnut tree. That knee of his wouldn't let him kneel; he could only shoot standing. Then he nocked an arrow, drew the bow only halfway, and simply held it there.

Xiaoman held his breath, waiting for him to draw, and he wouldn't draw.

A gust swept down the slope and the grass tips all lay flat together; he didn't move. The gust passed, the grass tips wavered twice and slowly rose — and in the instant when they were nearly upright but not quite, that patched bow in his hands came to full draw in one breath, bent like a crescent moon, and the moment it was full he loosed. There was a *whoosh*, and before the pheasant could so much as flap, it had turned over in the grass.

One arrow, one pheasant. Xiaoman ran over and picked it up. The arrow had gone clean through its neck, dead on the mark. His father took the arrow back and, before he even looked at the pheasant, wiped the head clean on his sleeve, held the shaft up to the light to see if it was still straight, and only then put it back in the quiver.

Xiaoman said, "Pa, you already had the arrow on the string. What were you waiting for?" His father said, "For the wind to catch its breath." Xiaoman said, "The wind catches its breath?" His father said, "Everything has to catch its breath. The wind does, deer do, people do." He paused, then said, "Ma San does too." Xiaoman didn't understand that at the time, but he felt it was the most learned thing his father had ever said in his life, and he fixed it firmly in his memory.

There was one more thing he fixed in his memory, but didn't say out loud. Yesterday evening, kneeling in front of Ma San, his father's two hands pressed on the ground had been shaking. Today, drawing this bow, his father's two hands had been steady as rock, and the bowstring hadn't so much as quivered. So his father's hands hadn't been born shaking after all.

Xiaoman said, "Pa, what about the second arrow?" His father said, "Next year." Which was the same as saying nothing, and on that point, Xiaoman felt, his father was a little like Granny Wu.

Xiaoman wouldn't give up. He thought: if he couldn't draw the bow, he could at least read the wind. Before they'd gone far he copied his father, plucked a hair from his head, held it up by one end, and waited to see which way it would float. Float it did — not east, and not west. A gust came, and it floated straight into his father's mouth. His father went *ptoo, ptoo, ptoo*, spat seven or eight times in a row, scraped his tongue over and over with a finger, and only then turned round, his dark face pulled very long, and glared at him.

Xiaoman said, "Pa, the wind's blowing your way." His father said, "…So I gather."

By noon the near hills hadn't shown them a second living thing. That pheasant was the whole of the morning's take for father and son — skin and bone, like carrying a mop in your arms. One pheasant couldn't stand in for a deer hide. His father sat on a rock rubbing his knee and didn't say anything for a long time.

Xiaoman couldn't keep still. He climbed another pine to look. The near hills were bare, nothing there; further in, two ridges away, lay a pine forest, black and dense. That was Black Pine Ridge. He was about to slide down when something moved at the edge of the forest. First read the wind — the treetops leaned behind him; the wind was blowing from the forest towards him.

He held his breath and looked again: under the black pines a reddish-brown shape that had had its head down slowly raised it, and on top of its head stood up a cluster of something, like bare winter branches. In the blink of an eye the shape turned and was gone into the forest.

"Pa, there's a deer."

His father was on his feet at once, knee or no knee. One deer was one deer hide and twenty catties of meat; it was the bow on the wall. Father and son fixed the direction and felt their way over, crossed two ridges, and came to the edge of the forest. Sure enough there was a line of fresh hoof prints in the mud, big and deep, heading into the trees. They followed the prints through a thicket of thorn scrub, and in front of them stood a broken stone.
